planting.note: Plant rooted dormant cuttings in spring on the high, stony limestone benches of the Bekaa Valley; vines are traditionally dry-farmed at altitude (roughly 3,000 feet) with minimal irrigation.

directions: Obaideh is one of Lebanon's two ancient native white grapes, grown for centuries on old, ungrafted bush vines across the high plateau of the Bekaa Valley and best known internationally as one of the two varieties blended into Chateau Musar's distinctive barrel-aged white wine. The grape buds and ripens early relative to its usual blending partner Merwah, developing good sugar despite the vineyard's thin, rocky, lime-rich soils and near-total reliance on winter rainfall rather than irrigation. Because the variety is rare outside a handful of old Lebanese plots, growers interested in it should source budwood or rooted cuttings directly from Lebanese or specialist heritage-grape collections rather than commercial nurseries. Give it a hot, dry, full-sun site with sharp drainage and minimal fertility, training low as an unirrigated bush vine in the traditional Bekaa style.
sources: Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding & Jose Vouillamoz, Wine Grapes (2012)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring on dry, rocky, high-altitude sites in Mount Lebanon or the Bekaa; Merwah ripens later than its usual blending partner Obaideh and needs a long warm autumn to finish.

directions: Merwah is the second of Lebanon's two ancient indigenous white grapes, long grown on unirrigated bush vines in the hill country of Mount Lebanon and the Bekaa Valley and sometimes nicknamed the 'Lebanese Semillon' for the waxy, lanolin-tinged richness it can develop with age. It is more aromatic and slower-ripening than its usual blending partner Obaideh, and small Lebanese producers also bottle it unblended into rustic, amber-gold, slightly oxidative white wines. The vine is tolerant of poor, stony, lime-rich soils and summer drought but is cold-sensitive and needs a long, dry, hot growing season to reach full ripeness. Source cuttings from Lebanese heritage vineyards or specialist grape collections, plant on a sunny, well-drained slope, and train low as a dry-farmed bush vine.
sources: Jancis Robinson, Julia Harding & Jose Vouillamoz, Wine Grapes (2012)

common_name: Maratheftiko Grape (Cypriot Heirloom Red Wine Grape)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring and train on a trellis rather than as a low bush vine; because Maratheftiko sets fruit poorly on its own, interplant with another Vitis vinifera variety nearby to supply pollen.

directions: Maratheftiko, also known locally as Vambakadha, is an ancient Cypriot red grape grown mainly in the hill villages of the Pitsilia and Larnaca districts but nearly abandoned in the twentieth century because its flowers have very poor self-fertility and fail to set a reliable crop unless a different grape variety is planted close by to provide pollen. Modern Cypriot winemakers have revived it over the last few decades, training it on wires or trellis instead of the old low bush form used for Xynisteri and Mavro, since it needs better air flow and a longer hang time to ripen its thick, deeply pigmented skins. The resulting wines are notably more tannic, structured, and age-worthy than Cyprus's traditional pale reds, and the variety is now considered the island's flagship fine-wine red grape. Give it full sun, low-fertility rocky or clay-limestone soil, minimal irrigation, and a nearby pollenizer vine for fruit set.

common_name: Sein Ta Lone Mango (Burmese Heirloom Mango)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun in deep, well-drained soil; Sein Ta Lone is Myanmar's most celebrated dessert mango, grown mainly in the dry-zone orchards of Mandalay and Sagaing regions.

directions: Sein Ta Lone, whose name translates roughly as 'single diamond,' is widely regarded in Myanmar as the country's finest dessert mango, grown chiefly in the hot, dry orchards of the Mandalay and Sagaing regions where intense dry-season heat concentrates the fruit's sugars. The fruit is small to medium, golden-skinned with a faint blush, and valued for exceptionally sweet, fiberless, melting flesh around a thin, flat seed, ripening in the hot pre-monsoon months. Trees are grafted onto seedling rootstock, grow vigorously in full sun, and need deep, well-drained soil with a distinct dry season to concentrate flavor the way they do in their native dry zone. Protect young trees from any cold and water moderately through establishment, then taper irrigation as fruit approaches ripeness to maximize sweetness.
sources: Myanmar Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Irrigation — mango cultivar surveys
Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations — Myanmar fruit crop profiles

common_name: Shwebo Paw San Rice (Burmese Heirloom Fragrant Rice)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant seedlings into a warm, flooded paddy bed well after soil has warmed; Shwebo Paw San is grown traditionally around Shwebo in Myanmar's Sagaing Region and is considered the country's most prized aromatic rice.

directions: Shwebo Paw San is Myanmar's best-known fragrant rice, grown traditionally in paddies around the town of Shwebo in Sagaing Region and widely regarded within the country as the standard against which other aromatic rice is judged. The grains are short-to-medium, pearly white, and release a distinct sweet, buttery fragrance when cooked, making the variety the preferred choice for everyday steamed rice rather than pulao-style dishes. Plants are grown in standing water through most of the vegetative season in the hot, humid conditions of the monsoon-season rice calendar and are photoperiod-sensitive, flowering as daylength shortens in late summer. Gardeners outside Myanmar's climate will need a sheltered flooded paddy bed, full sun, and a monsoon-like warm, humid season or controlled daylength to coax the plant to head out and fill grain properly.
sources: Myanmar Rice Federation, Paw San variety documentation
International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) Genesys germplasm database

common_name: Suwandel Rice (Sri Lankan Heirloom Aromatic Rice)

planting.note: Direct sow into a warm, flooded paddy bed; Suwandel is a traditional short-season Sri Lankan lowland rice still maintained by heirloom seed savers and used especially for festive milk-rice (kiribath).

directions: Suwandel, whose name translates roughly as 'fragrant sandalwood,' is a traditional Sri Lankan short-grain aromatic rice landrace long grown in the island's wet and intermediate zones and now conserved mainly by heirloom seed networks rather than commercial agriculture. It is prized above most other Sri Lankan rices for ceremonial and festive cooking, especially kiribath (coconut milk rice) served at New Year and other celebrations, because of its delicate fragrance and soft, slightly sticky texture once cooked. The plant is relatively short-strawed and short-season compared with many other traditional Sri Lankan varieties, maturing within about four months of direct seeding into a flooded bed. Grow it in full sun with standing water through the vegetative stage, in the same warm, humid conditions as other tropical lowland rice.
sources: Department of Agriculture, Sri Lanka — traditional rice variety documentation
International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) Genesys germplasm database

common_name: Kalu Heenati Rice (Sri Lankan Heirloom Red Rice)

planting.note: Direct sow into a warm, flooded paddy bed; Kalu Heenati is a traditional Sri Lankan red-pericarp rice landrace valued in traditional and Ayurvedic cooking for its dark red bran layer.

directions: Kalu Heenati is a traditional Sri Lankan rice landrace named for its slender grain and dark reddish-black pericarp, a bran layer left intact when the rice is only lightly milled for traditional and Ayurvedic-style cooking such as herbal rice porridge (kola kenda). The variety is tall-strawed and lodging-prone compared with modern dwarf rices, reflecting its long cultivation history before the mid-twentieth-century shift to high-yield varieties, and it is now mostly kept alive by traditional-rice conservation programs and small growers rather than mainstream commercial paddies. Like other Sri Lankan lowland rices it needs standing water through most of its vegetative growth, full tropical sun, and a long warm season to fill its grain properly. Home growers outside the tropics will need a warm, flooded paddy bed and a long, humid growing season to replicate the conditions under which it has traditionally thrived.
sources: Department of Agriculture, Sri Lanka — traditional rice variety documentation
International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) Genesys germplasm database

planting.note: Direct sow into a warm, flooded paddy bed; Pachchaperumal is one of the traditional Sri Lankan rice landraces maintained today mainly through heirloom and traditional-rice conservation networks.

directions: Pachchaperumal is one of the traditional long-cultivated rice landraces of Sri Lanka's lowland paddy regions, grown historically for its hardiness in village cultivation systems before the widespread adoption of modern semi-dwarf varieties. Like its heirloom counterparts, it is tall-strawed, matures over a long tropical growing season, and is cultivated today mainly by traditional-rice seed keepers and small growers interested in preserving pre-Green-Revolution Sri Lankan genetic diversity rather than by large commercial operations. It requires a standing-water paddy environment through most of its vegetative growth and full, strong tropical sun to fill its grain. Outside Sri Lanka's monsoon-driven climate, growers will need a warm, humid, long-season flooded bed to bring the plant through to harvest.
sources: Department of Agriculture, Sri Lanka — traditional rice variety documentation
International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) Genesys germplasm database
